items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose an insurance company offers two different products and wants to determine whether the proportion of satisfied customers on each plan differs. One way to do this is to take a random sample of customers on each plan, find each plan's proportion of satisfied customers, and then calculate a confidence interval for the difference between the two proportions.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to construct a confidence for the difference between two population proportions.

Content:
Suppose we have two populations: population [MATH: 1] and population [MATH: 2.] Let the proportion of individuals in the first and second populations with a particular characteristic be [MATH: p_1] and [MATH: p_2,] respectively. Independent random samples of size [MATH: n_1] and [MATH: n_2] are drawn from each population.

Content:
If the sample sizes are sufficiently large such that
[MATH: n_i \cdot \widehat{\,p}_i > 5, \qquad n_i\cdot (1-\widehat{\,p}_i)>5, \qquad i=1,2,]
then, we know that the sampling distributions of our estimates [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_2] of [MATH: p_1] and [MATH: p_2] respectively are given by
[MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1 \sim N\left(p_1, \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}\right), \qquad \widehat{\,p}_2 \sim N\left(p_2, \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}\right).]

Content:
Since the samples are independent, by the properties of expectation and variance, we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E [\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] = p_1 - p_2, \qquad \textrm{Var} [\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] = \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_2] are normally distributed, their difference is also normal, and we have
[MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2 \sim N\left(p_1 - p_2, \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}\right)]

Content:
In most practical situations, [MATH: p_1] and [MATH: p_2] are unknown. However, we can approximate the above distribution using estimates obtained from sample data. Thus, we can write

Content:
[MATH: Z= \dfrac{(\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2) - (p_1-p_2)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2)}{n_2}}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1).]

Content:
Let's now look at how we can use this information to construct confidence intervals for differences in proportions.

Given that the samples are independent and the sample proportions of individuals having the characteristic in the two samples are, respectively, [MATH: \widehat{p}_1=0.52] and [MATH: \widehat{p}_2=0.5,] find a [MATH: 98\%] confidence interval for the difference [MATH: p_1-p_2] between the corresponding population proportions.

Hint: Use the fact that [MATH: P(Z > 2.326) = 0.01,] where [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1),] as shown in the diagram above.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since [MATH: n_1=75,] [MATH: n_2=62,] [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1=0.52] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_2=0.5,] we have that

  • [MATH: n_1 \widehat{\,p}_1 = 75\cdot 0.52 = 39> 5,]

  • [MATH: n_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1) = 75\cdot (1-0.52) = 36> 5,]

  • [MATH: n_2 \widehat{\,p}_2 = 62\cdot 0.5 = 31> 5,]

  • [MATH: n_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2) = 62\cdot (1-0.5) = 31> 5.]

As a result, we may use a normal approximation:

[MATH: \dfrac{(\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2) - (p_1-p_2)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2)}{n_2}}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1),]

where

  • [MATH: \!\widehat{\,p}_1, \widehat{\,p}_2] are the sample proportions,

  • [MATH: p_1, p_2] are the population proportions,

  • [MATH: n_1, n_2] are the sample sizes.

Then, given a value [MATH: \alpha] between [MATH: 0] and [MATH: 1,] the corresponding [MATH: [100(1-\alpha)]\%] confidence interval for the population difference of proportions [MATH: p_1-p_2] can be written as

[MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1-\widehat{\,p}_2 \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2)}{n_2}},]

where [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

We are interested in finding a [MATH: 98\%] confidence interval. So, we have

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.98=0.02 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.01.]

We are given that [MATH: P(Z > 2.326) = 0.01.] As a result,

[MATH: z_{\alpha/2} = z_{0.01} = 2.326.]

Therefore, a [MATH: 98\%] confidence interval for the difference of the population proportions [MATH: p_1-p_2] is the following:

[MATH: (0.52 − 0.5) ± 2.326 ⋅ sqrt((0.52(1 − 0.52))/(75) + (0.5(1 − 0.5))/(62))]

which simplifies as

[MATH: 0.02 ± 0.20.]

Finally, the confidence interval is [MATH: (0.02 - 0.20, \, 0.02 + 0.20) = \left( -0.18, 0.22\right).]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose an insurance company offers two different products and wants to determine whether the proportion of satisfied customers on each plan differs. One way to do this is to take a random sample of customers on each plan, find each plan's proportion of satisfied customers, and then calculate a confidence interval for the difference between the two proportions.

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to construct a confidence for the difference between two population proportions.

Content:
Suppose we have two populations: population [MATH: 1] and population [MATH: 2.] Let the proportion of individuals in the first and second populations with a particular characteristic be [MATH: p_1] and [MATH: p_2,] respectively. Independent random samples of size [MATH: n_1] and [MATH: n_2] are drawn from each population.

Content:
If the sample sizes are sufficiently large such that
[MATH: n_i \cdot \widehat{\,p}_i > 5, \qquad n_i\cdot (1-\widehat{\,p}_i)>5, \qquad i=1,2,]
then, we know that the sampling distributions of our estimates [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_2] of [MATH: p_1] and [MATH: p_2] respectively are given by
[MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1 \sim N\left(p_1, \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1}\right), \qquad \widehat{\,p}_2 \sim N\left(p_2, \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}\right).]

Content:
Since the samples are independent, by the properties of expectation and variance, we have

Content:
[MATH: \textrm E [\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] = p_1 - p_2, \qquad \textrm{Var} [\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2] = \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_2] are normally distributed, their difference is also normal, and we have
[MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2 \sim N\left(p_1 - p_2, \dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}\right)]

Content:
In most practical situations, [MATH: p_1] and [MATH: p_2] are unknown. However, we can approximate the above distribution using estimates obtained from sample data. Thus, we can write

Content:
[MATH: Z= \dfrac{(\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2) - (p_1-p_2)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2)}{n_2}}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1).]

Content:

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since [MATH: n_1=75,] [MATH: n_2=62,] [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1=0.52] and [MATH: \widehat{\,p}_2=0.5,] we have that

- [MATH: n_1 \widehat{\,p}_1 = 75\cdot 0.52 = 39> 5,]
- [MATH: n_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1) = 75\cdot (1-0.52) = 36> 5,]
- [MATH: n_2 \widehat{\,p}_2 = 62\cdot 0.5 = 31> 5,]
- [MATH: n_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2) = 62\cdot (1-0.5) = 31> 5.]

As a result, we may use a normal approximation:

[MATH: \dfrac{(\widehat{\,p}_1 - \widehat{\,p}_2) - (p_1-p_2)}{\sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2)}{n_2}}\phantom{|}} \sim N(0,1),]

- [MATH: \!\widehat{\,p}_1, \widehat{\,p}_2] are the sample proportions,
- [MATH: p_1, p_2] are the population proportions,
- [MATH: n_1, n_2] are the sample sizes.

[MATH: \widehat{\,p}_1-\widehat{\,p}_2 \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_1(1-\widehat{\,p}_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\widehat{\,p}_2(1-\widehat{\,p}_2)}{n_2}},]

where [MATH: P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \dfrac{\alpha}{2}] and [MATH: Z \sim N(0,1).]

[MATH: \alpha=1-0.98=0.02 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\dfrac{\alpha}{2}=0.01.]

[MATH: (0.52 − 0.5) ± 2.326 ⋅ sqrt((0.52(1 − 0.52))/(75) + (0.5(1 − 0.5))/(62))]

[MATH: 0.02 ± 0.20.]

[MATH: (0.02 - 0.20, \, 0.02 + 0.20) = \left( -0.18, 0.22\right).]
